course: Convert a Car Engine to an Irrigation Water Pump

lessons.title: L1
lessons.body: Before you touch a single bolt, you must plan. Engine removal is not a race; it is a careful process. First, park the vehicle on a flat, hard surface like a concrete slab. If you don't have concrete, use thick wooden planks under the wheels to prevent sinking. Engage the handbrake and chock the wheels. Disconnect the battery: remove the negative terminal first, then the positive. This prevents accidental sparks. Next, drain all fluids. Place a clean container under the oil drain plug (usually a 17mm or 19mm bolt) and remove it. Let the oil drain completelyâit may take 15 minutes. Do the same for the coolant: open the radiator drain cock or remove the lower hose. Be careful, coolant is toxic. Also drain the power steering fluid if equipped. Label and bag every bolt you remove. Use zip-lock bags and a permanent marker. Write where they came from, e.g., 'exhaust manifold bolts'. This saves hours later. Take photos with your phone before disconnecting anything. In rural Africa, you may not have a phone, so sketch the layout on paper. Note the firing order of spark plug wires. Remove the hood (bonnet) if it helps accessâtwo people can lift it. Remove the radiator and fan shroud. Keep the radiator upright to avoid bending fins. Disconnect the throttle cable, choke cable, and any electrical connectors. Use masking tape to label wires. If the engine is seized or you plan to convert it, you still need to remove it carefully. Work methodically. A clean removal makes the conversion easier. Remember, you are not just pulling an engine; you are preparing it for a new life as an irrigation pump.

lessons.title: L2
lessons.body: You will need a hoist or a strong lifting frame. In many African workshops, a simple A-frame made from 4-inch steel pipes or hardwood logs works well. The frame must support at least 500 kg. Use a chain hoist or a 2-ton come-along. Never use rope that can stretch or snap. Attach the hoist to the engine lifting eyes or use a lifting chain bolted to the cylinder head boltsâremove two head bolts and screw in lifting eyes. If you don't have lifting eyes, use a thick nylon sling rated for 1 ton. Position the hoist directly above the engine. Take up the slack slowly. Remove the engine mount boltsâusually two on each side, 14mm or 17mm. Also unbolt the transmission bell housing from the engine block. Support the transmission with a jack or wooden blocks so it doesn't hang. Remove the starter motor (two or three bolts). Disconnect the exhaust pipe from the manifold. Now, lift the engine slowly. Watch for anything still attached: wires, hoses, linkages. Have a helper guide the engine as it comes out. Once clear, lower it onto a sturdy pallet or old tires. Never let it drop. If you are working alone, use a chain fall and go slowly. After removal, mount the engine on a stand or a heavy wooden bench. This is your preparation station. Clean the engine with a wire brush and diesel. Remove the clutch and flywheel if you don't need themâthey are not needed for a pump. Keep the flywheel if you plan to use a belt drive; it provides momentum. But for direct coupling, remove it. Also remove the alternator, starter, and air conditioning compressor. You won't need them. Keep the water pump if it is in good condition; otherwise, you will replace it. The goal is a bare engine block with cylinder head, ready for the next steps.

lessons.title: L3
lessons.body: Once the engine is out, strip it down to the long block. Start by removing the intake and exhaust manifolds. These are held by 12mm or 14mm bolts. Soak them with penetrating oil like WD-40 if they are rusty. Wait 10 minutes, then turn slowly. If a bolt snaps, you will need to drill it outâavoid that. Next, remove the valve cover (usually 10mm bolts). Inspect the rocker arms and pushrods. If they are worn, replace them. Remove the cylinder head bolts in the correct sequence: start from the outside and work inward in a spiral pattern. Use a breaker bar. Once the head is off, check the head gasket for cracks. Clean the block deck with a scraper and sandpaper. Now remove the oil pan (10mm or 12mm bolts). Clean out sludge with diesel and a brush. Remove the oil pump and pickup tube. For a pump application, you might keep the oil pump to circulate oil, but often you will block it off. Remove the timing cover and timing chain or belt. If the engine is a pushrod type, remove the camshaft. If overhead cam, remove the cam caps evenly. Keep all valvetrain parts in orderâuse a cardboard template to store pushrods and rockers. Remove the pistons and connecting rods if you plan to rebuild. For a pump, you may keep the pistons to maintain compression, but if the engine is worn, a rebuild is wise. Hone the cylinders if needed. Replace all gaskets and seals. This is the time to install new bearings, piston rings, and a new timing chain. A clean, well-sealed engine will run cooler and last longer. Work in a shaded area to avoid overheating. Use a torque wrench for all critical bolts. If you don't have one, borrow or buy a cheap oneâit is essential.

lessons.title: L4
lessons.body: A car engine is designed to run at variable speeds, but an irrigation pump needs a steady speed. You must remove or modify the governor. Most car engines have a mechanical governor inside the distributor or carburetor. For a pump, you will likely convert to a fixed throttle setting. Remove the carburetor and intake manifold. You will replace the carburetor with a simple throttle body or a fixed venturi. If you keep the carburetor, wire the throttle open to a set positionâabout 1500 to 2000 RPM for a small pump. But better: remove the distributor and install a electronic ignition system or a magneto. You need a reliable spark. For diesel engines, you will adjust the injection pump to a fixed rack setting. This is more complex; consider a diesel if you have one because they are more fuel-efficient and have more torque. For petrol engines, remove the mechanical fuel pump and install an electric fuel pump (low pressure, 3-5 psi). You will also need to remove the radiator fan and replace it with an electric fan or a direct-coupled fan. But for a pump, you may not need a fan if the engine runs at low speed and has a large water tank. Remove the air filter housing; you will install a simple mesh filter. Now, the most important part: the output shaft. You need to connect the engine's crankshaft to the pump. Remove the flywheel and clutch. The crankshaft flange will have 6 or 8 bolt holes. You will bolt a pulley or a coupling to this flange. For a belt drive, use a double-groove pulley. For direct coupling, use a flexible coupling like a Lovejoy coupling. Align it perfectlyâmisalignment causes vibration and bearing failure. Use a dial indicator if available, or a straight edge. Also, remove the power steering pump and air conditioning compressorâthey rob power. Block off any vacuum lines. The engine should now be a bare, self-contained power unit. Test it on a stand with fuel and ignition before mounting the pump.

lessons.title: L5
lessons.body: Preparation is everything. After stripping the engine, you must clean and inspect every part. Use a parts washer or a bucket of diesel and a stiff brush. Scrape off old gaskets with a putty knife. Do not gouge the aluminum surfaces. For the cylinder head, check for warping with a straight edge and feeler gauge. If it is warped more than 0.05mm, have it resurfaced at a machine shop. Check the cylinder walls for scoring. If there are deep scratches, you need to rebore and install oversize pistons. That is expensive. For a pump, a slightly worn engine can still work, but it will burn oil. If you can afford it, do a rebuild. Replace all bearings: main bearings, rod bearings, and cam bearings. Use plastigauge to check clearance. Install new piston rings. Hone the cylinders with a ball hone to create a cross-hatch pattern. This helps rings seal. Clean the block thoroughly with soap and water, then dry with compressed air. Oil the cylinder walls immediately to prevent rust. Now, assemble the engine with new gaskets. Use a torque wrench in the correct sequence. For the cylinder head, torque in three steps: 30 Nm, 60 Nm, then 90 Nm, following the manual. If you don't have a manual, search online for your engine model. For a typical 4-cylinder, head bolts are torqued to about 80-100 Nm. Install a new timing belt or chain. Set the timing marks perfectly. Install the oil pump and new oil filter. Fill with 15W-40 diesel engine oil (for diesel) or 20W-50 for petrol. Prime the oil system by cranking the engine with the coil disconnected until oil pressure builds. Then start it. Let it idle for 20 minutes, then change oil and filter again. This removes assembly debris. Now the engine is ready for the pump coupling. Remember, a clean engine is a reliable engine.

lessons.title: L6
lessons.body: You have removed and prepared the engine. Now you must connect it to the pump. But before that, build a sturdy base. Use a steel frame made from 50mm angle iron. Weld or bolt it together. The base must be level and strong enough to handle vibration. Mount the engine on rubber isolators to reduce vibration. Now, align the engine output shaft with the pump input shaft. If using a belt drive, mount the pump on a sliding rail so you can tension the belts. Use a double V-belt for reliability. Align the pulleys with a straight edgeâthey must be parallel and in line. For direct coupling, use a flexible coupling. The two shafts must be aligned within 0.05mm. Use a dial indicator to check. If you don't have one, use a feeler gauge between the coupling halves. Rotate the engine by hand and check for binding. Now, connect the plumbing. The pump inlet should have a strainer and a foot valve. Use a 2-inch suction hose for a 2-inch pump. The discharge line should have a check valve and a gate valve. For irrigation, you might use lay-flat hose or PVC pipes. Ensure all connections are tightâair leaks on the suction side will stop the pump from priming. Prime the pump by filling the casing with water. Start the engine and let it run at 1500 RPM. Adjust the throttle until the pump delivers the desired flow. For a typical 5 HP engine, you can expect about 500 liters per minute at 10 meters head. Monitor temperature and oil pressure. After 30 minutes, check for leaks and tighten bolts. Now you have a working irrigation pump. Maintain it: change oil every 100 hours, clean the air filter, and check belts. This engine will serve you for years if treated well.

quiz.q: What is the first step before removing an engine?
quiz.explanation: Disconnecting the battery prevents accidental sparks and electrical damage.

quiz.q: Which tool is essential for lifting an engine safely?
quiz.explanation: A chain hoist is rated for heavy loads and will not stretch or snap.

quiz.q: What should you use to label bolts and parts?
quiz.explanation: Bagging and labeling bolts prevents confusion during reassembly.

quiz.q: Why should you take photos before disconnecting wires?
quiz.explanation: Photos serve as a reference for reconnecting wires correctly.

quiz.q: What is the correct order to disconnect battery terminals?
quiz.explanation: Disconnecting the negative terminal first prevents short circuits.

quiz.q: What should you do with the radiator after removal?
quiz.explanation: Keeping the radiator upright prevents bending the cooling fins.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT needed for a pump conversion?
quiz.explanation: The alternator is not needed for a stationary pump engine.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of removing the clutch and flywheel?
options: B) To access the crankshaft flange
quiz.explanation: The crankshaft flange is used to couple the pump.

quiz.q: What should you use to clean engine parts?
quiz.explanation: Diesel is a safe and effective solvent for grease and grime.

quiz.q: What is the correct torque sequence for cylinder head bolts?
quiz.explanation: Spiral pattern from outside inward prevents warping.

quiz.q: What tool is essential for tightening critical bolts?
quiz.explanation: A torque wrench ensures bolts are tightened to specification.

quiz.q: Why should you replace the timing chain or belt?
quiz.explanation: A worn timing chain can break and cause engine damage.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of honing cylinders?
options: B) To create cross-hatch for ring seating
quiz.explanation: Cross-hatch helps piston rings seal against the cylinder wall.

quiz.q: What should you do after assembling an engine?
quiz.explanation: Priming the oil system prevents dry start damage.

quiz.q: What is the typical oil pressure for a small engine?
quiz.explanation: Most engines run 30-60 psi at operating temperature.

quiz.q: What should you use to check cylinder head warpage?
options: B) Straight edge and feeler gauge
quiz.explanation: A straight edge and feeler gauge measure gaps indicating warpage.

quiz.q: What is the maximum allowable warpage for a cylinder head?
quiz.explanation: More than 0.05mm requires resurfacing.

quiz.q: What type of coupling is best for direct engine-to-pump connection?
quiz.explanation: Flexible coupling accommodates slight misalignment.

quiz.q: What is the recommended speed for a pump engine?
quiz.explanation: Most pumps operate efficiently at 1500-2000 RPM.

quiz.q: What should you use to reduce engine vibration?
quiz.explanation: Rubber isolators absorb vibration and protect the frame.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a foot valve?
quiz.explanation: A foot valve prevents water from draining back, maintaining prime.

quiz.q: How often should you change engine oil in a pump?
quiz.explanation: Regular oil changes every 100 hours prolong engine life.

quiz.q: What is the first step in aligning a belt drive?
quiz.explanation: Misaligned pulleys cause belt wear and vibration.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of pump failure to prime?
options: B) Air leak in suction line
quiz.explanation: Air leaks prevent suction and priming.

quiz.q: What size suction hose for a 2-inch pump?
quiz.explanation: Match hose size to pump inlet to avoid restriction.

quiz.q: What should you do before starting a newly assembled engine?
options: B) Crank without ignition to prime oil
quiz.explanation: Cranking without ignition builds oil pressure before firing.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a check valve in discharge line?
quiz.explanation: Check valve stops water from flowing back when pump stops.

quiz.q: What should you do after first 20 minutes of running a new engine?
quiz.explanation: Changing oil removes assembly debris and break-in particles.

quiz.q: What is the typical flow rate for a 5 HP pump at 10m head?
quiz.explanation: A 5 HP engine can deliver about 500 liters per minute at 10 meters head.

quiz.q: What should you do with unused vacuum lines?
quiz.explanation: Blocking vacuum lines prevents air leaks and rough running.
